data.body:
## A Decision We Can Explain

**Grade 6 · Four sessions with your teacher · One personal portfolio**

How can another person's idea help you make a decision you can explain? Use one fictional reading-space case to practice explaining, responding, using feedback and reflecting.

**Choose this unit or the shorter Thinking Together lesson.** They use the same case; you do not need to complete both. Plan about 35–45 minutes per session, with more time or split sessions when needed.

**Feeling like a lot?** Start small: pick one of the two starting plans on the Case Sheet, choose one fact, say one reason, and answer one thing your partner says. That is a complete start in any lesson.

**Want more challenge?** Anyone can try one: make the strongest case for the plan you did not choose, design a fair test of whether a divider blocks sound, or find a plan that uses all 6 tokens and name its tradeoff.

### Your four steps

1. **Clarify the goal.** Read the case, explain a starting idea, and agree how to exchange ideas. Portfolio **rows 1–2**.
2. **Exchange ideas.** Respond to a partner and make a working decision. Portfolio **rows 3–4**.
3. **Use feedback.** Check one part of your work, try a next version, and explain why. Portfolio **rows 5–6**.
4. **Reflect.** Explain your thinking now, compare it with your first try, and choose a next step. Portfolio **rows 7–8**.

**Case Sheet:** **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** has all the facts, prices and success criteria. Keep it open during every lesson and while you use your portfolio.

**Your record:** Open **My Decision Portfolio** for two rows each session. Short notes or references to work in your usual format are enough. Keep earlier entries. Summary and Connections are optional. The Lesson 3 pictures have full captions, so you can use the captions with or without the pictures.

**Sentence starters and word help:** Open **Sentence Starters for Explaining and Responding** or **Words for This Unit** in any lesson. Use a whole starter, part of one, or your own words.

**Navigation:** Start with Lesson 1 below. Open **My Resources**, then return to this Unit Map to open the next lesson or your portfolio. Your teacher can use the separate Teacher Guide before the first session.

**More practice later:** Your teacher can open the separate pack **Thinking Together: More Practice** for six optional follow-up routes, including one where you bring a real class decision.

### Credit

Adapted from ideas in three articles by Katie Novak, published by Novak Education:

- [“Communicating High Expectations to Learners”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/communicating-high-expectations-to-learners) (2024): Lessons 1 and 3.
- [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (2026): Lesson 2.
- [“It’s Always Time for Student Self-Reflection”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/student-self-reflection) (2025): Lesson 4.

This is an original AlloFlow unit; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it. The articles are written for teachers, so students do not need to read them.

history.title: Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision
history.meta: Reference for all four lessons | Facts, prices, starting plans and success criteria | Keep it open
history.data:
## Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision

**Use with all four lessons and your portfolio.** Keep this sheet open while you work.

### The fictional case

A school is changing one reading corner. Your group can spend **at most 6 equipment tokens**. Use the evidence below to decide what to choose. You may also propose a routine that costs no tokens. Every fact, number and price in this case is made up for practice.

**Evidence A: Preferences.** In a fictional class of 30, 24 selected a quiet place for independent reading and 18 selected a place to discuss a book with a partner. They could select both choices, so do not add the counts to find a class total.

**Evidence B: A space check.** In the trial layout, a large fixed table blocked the route to one shelf. Any new plan must keep a clear route to every shelf. The teacher will check the actual layout before use.

**Evidence C: A sound check.** During three practice sessions, partner talk could be heard across this small corner. No one has tested whether a divider would reduce that sound.

**Evidence D: A light check.** The existing corner light does not reach every reading position. The room already has another well-lit reading area.

**Evidence E: Available equipment.** A divider costs 3 tokens; a task lamp costs 2; a movable table costs 3; a book basket costs 1; a set of seat pads costs 2. Choose each item at most once. A divider can mark two areas but is not guaranteed to block sound. A movable table can be repositioned; its fit must be checked. A basket can bring books closer; it must not block the route. Seat pads add floor-seating choices, but floor seating is optional. A lamp adds light at one position; check cords and placement before use.

### Two starting plans, if helpful

- **Lamp + basket:** 2 + 1 = **3 tokens**.
- **Divider + basket:** 3 + 1 = **4 tokens**.

For either plan, you may propose separate times for quiet reading and partner discussion. Compare these two plans, or create your own pair using Evidence E. You do not need to compare every possible combination. These are starting ideas, not model answers.

### What makes our work useful? Check your own work

- **Reasoning:** I can compare two plans and explain how two case facts support my choice.
- **Case checks:** I can show a total of 6 tokens or fewer with each item chosen once, say how I would check the shelf routes, and name one question that is still open. I don’t claim something works when no one has tested it.
- **Responding:** I can check that I understood what my partner actually said, answer it, and show what my reply changes or leaves open.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Communicating High Expectations to Learners”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/communicating-high-expectations-to-learners) (Novak Education, 2024). This is an original AlloFlow case sheet; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

## Lesson 1: What would make our decision convincing?

**Lesson 1 of 4 · Grade 6 · With your teacher**

**Today:** Read the case, explain your starting idea, and keep it so you can look back later. Complete portfolio rows **1 · First response** and **2 · Criteria and access**.

Across four lessons, you will explain a choice, consider another idea, use feedback and reflect. More than one plan can work. Your reasons matter more than finding a particular shopping list. This is real grade 6 work, and you can do it. The supports are here to help.

**Warm-up (2 minutes):** Think of a time someone else’s idea changed your mind, or helped you explain your own idea better. Share it with your partner in any way you like, or just keep it in mind.

### Read the case

Open **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision**. Read it with a partner, with your teacher, or with your reading supports. It has the facts (Evidence A–E), the prices, two starting plans, and the three things we look for in useful work: **Reasoning**, **Case checks** and **Responding**. Keep it open for the whole unit.

### 1. Keep your starting idea

Use Evidence A–E and the **Reasoning** and **Case checks** criteria from the Case Sheet. In **1 · First response**, compare two plans and recommend one. Include its cost, two facts with your reasons, and a remaining check. Short notes or an explanation in your usual format are enough.

Work on your own thinking, with the supports you need. Ask about unfamiliar words or directions, or check **Words for This Unit**. Mark anything you can't answer yet. This first try is not graded. Save it before you look at examples or get feedback on it.

### 2. Make the criteria clear together

With a partner or educator, choose one criterion from the Case Sheet. Suggest an example of what it would look like in this task and agree on its meaning. Record that example in **2 · Criteria and access**. Add one personal discussion goal for the unit, such as “I will check what my partner meant before I answer.”

In the same row, agree how you will send and receive ideas in Lesson 2. Send a practice message, such as “Can you read this?”, so you both know the method works. Writing back and forth is fine.

**Before you finish:** Can you find your saved first response, and can your partner receive your next message? Bring back one question if you need help.

**Ways to take part:** Write, type, sketch, speak, sign, or use a communication board or device (AAC), whichever works for you. Take time to prepare, and keep the reading, math and communication supports you need. If someone writes for you, check that they wrote what you meant. For work kept somewhere else, such as a recording or a drawing, add a short note in your portfolio saying where it is. Need words to start? Open **Sentence Starters for Explaining and Responding**.

**Find your way:** Open **My Resources**, then **Unit Map: Four Lessons, One Portfolio**, to reach your portfolio or another lesson. Do not delete earlier entries.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Communicating High Expectations to Learners”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/communicating-high-expectations-to-learners) (Novak Education, 2024). This is an original AlloFlow lesson; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

## Use another idea in a shared decision

**Today:** Practice a useful response, then compare plans with a partner. Complete portfolio rows **3 · Actual exchange** and **4 · Working decision**. An educator can be your partner.

**Case Sheet:** Keep **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** open for the facts, prices and success criteria. The budget is at most six tokens.

### 1. Notice a useful response

**Original fictional model:**

**Partner 1:** “A divider and lamp cost five tokens. I would choose them.”

**Partner 2:** “Will the divider stop the sound? No one has tested that in this corner.”

**Partner 1:** “That is uncertain. We could compare my plan with a lamp, basket and separate reading/discussion times.”

**Partner 2:** “Let's compare both costs and the shelf-route checks before deciding.”

Point to a reply that takes up the other person's idea. What does it help the pair check? If Partner 2 had only named a favorite item, what would still need a response? Try one useful reply together before starting your own exchange.

### 2. Exchange your own ideas

Take 1–2 minutes to prepare your proposal and a reason. *Option: split the evidence.* One partner becomes the expert on Evidence A–C (who uses the corner, the space and the sound); the other on Evidence D–E (the light and the equipment). Then your working decision needs both of you. Share your ideas through your agreed method. Your partner asks about or responds to that reason; answer their actual reply. Switch who starts so both people contribute and respond.

In **3 · Actual exchange**, keep one short chain: **my idea → partner's reply → my response**. Check with your partner that your notes say what each of you meant. If a reply has not arrived, write “still waiting” and arrange another opportunity.

### 3. Make a working decision together

Compare at least two plans. In **4 · Working decision**, record:

- your recommendation and cost;
- two case facts and why they support it;
- what your partner's idea helped you change, clarify or question;
- one check still needed.

You may keep an earlier proposal with reasons. If you disagree, record the two positions and a next check instead of pretending to agree. Each learner keeps a copy or reference to the shared decision in their own portfolio.

**Before you finish:** Point to an actual reply. What did it make clearer, and what is still open? If a reply is still missing, name the next opportunity. The recommendation may still need testing.

**Ways to take part:** Write, type, sketch, speak, sign, or use a communication board or device (AAC), whichever works for you. Take time to prepare, and keep the reading, math and communication supports you need. If someone writes for you, check that they wrote what you meant. For work kept somewhere else, such as a recording or a drawing, add a short note in your portfolio saying where it is. Need words to start? Open **Sentence Starters for Explaining and Responding**.

**Find your way:** Open **My Resources**, then **Unit Map: Four Lessons, One Portfolio**, to reach your portfolio or another lesson. Do not delete earlier entries.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). This is an original AlloFlow lesson; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

panels.title: Keep a proposal—with reasons
panels.caption:
**The situation:** Partner 1 wants a lamp and basket (3 tokens): some reading spots are dark, and a basket brings books closer. Partner 2 wants a divider and basket (4 tokens): the class wants both quiet reading and partner talk, and a divider can mark two areas. The room has another well-lit reading area. Nobody has tested whether a divider blocks sound.

**Partner 1 could keep the plan:** “You want separate areas for quiet reading and partner talk. I still choose the lamp and basket, because some reading spots here are dark and a lamp can light one of them. Your idea makes me ask how we will fit in both kinds of reading. Nobody has tested the sound yet, and we still need to check the cord, where things go, and the paths to the shelves. What have I missed?”

**Compare both replies:** In each one, find (1) the partner’s idea it answers, (2) a case fact and why it matters, and (3) something still to check. Both replies are reasonable; neither is the one right answer.

**Your turn in Lesson 3:** Ask a partner or teacher to look at your own work. Write their feedback and your next try in **My Decision Portfolio**.

Use case: scientific-educational
Asset type: illustration for a middle-school discussion activity, justified retention of a proposal after considering another idea.
Create a left-to-right objects-only comparison. On the left, one teal paper proposal card showing exactly a simple desk lamp and a small handled basket containing books. In the middle, a smaller ochre paper speech-bubble card shows a freestanding rectangular room divider and a book basket: this is a counterproposal. Two broad navy paper paths from these cards converge toward an open cream notebook on the right. panels.title: Revise a proposal—with reasons
panels.caption:
**The situation:** Partner 1 wants a lamp and basket (3 tokens): some reading spots are dark, and a basket brings books closer. Partner 2 wants a divider and basket (4 tokens): the class wants both quiet reading and partner talk, and a divider can mark two areas. The room has another well-lit reading area. Nobody has tested whether a divider blocks sound.

**Partner 1 could change the plan:** “You want separate areas for quiet reading and partner talk. I now choose the divider and basket. Evidence A shows many students want both a quiet place and a place to talk, and a divider can mark two areas. Evidence D reminded me there is another well-lit reading area. We still need to check the light and the paths to the shelves, and nobody knows yet if a divider blocks sound. What have I missed?”

**Compare both replies:** In each one, find (1) the partner’s idea it answers, (2) a case fact and why it matters, and (3) something still to check. Both replies are reasonable; neither is the one right answer.

**Your turn in Lesson 3:** Ask a partner or teacher to look at your own work. Write their feedback and your next try in **My Decision Portfolio**.

history.data:
## Use feedback and try again

**Today:** Ask for feedback on one part of your decision and use it. Complete portfolio rows **5 · Checked feedback** and **6 · Next version + why**. Keep your earlier decision available.

**Case Sheet:** Keep **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** open for the facts and prices.

### 1. Compare two possible responses

Open **Keep or Change? Two Example Replies** from the Unit Map. Read the captions, with or without the pictures. Find a received idea, a reason and a remaining check in each. One example keeps a proposal; the other changes it. Either can involve careful thinking. These invented replies are examples, not your own feedback record.

### 2. Ask about one part of your work

Choose **Reasoning** (how facts support a choice) or **Case checks** (cost, shelf routes and untested effects). Point to one place in your working decision and tell a partner or educator what you want them to check.

The reviewer names something they notice and suggests one next action or asks a useful question. Your reviewer will be honest and specific, because they know you can reach the goal. Check that you understand their feedback. In **5 · Checked feedback**, write the criterion you chose, where in your work they looked, what they said and what you think it means. Ask the reviewer to confirm or correct what you wrote. If there is time, switch roles with a peer.

### 3. Try it and show why

In **6 · Next version + why**, write the part you changed, or explain why you kept it. Use a case fact to support your choice and name what still needs checking. Keep the earlier version too; you do not need to copy the whole recommendation again.

Show the reviewer what you tried. Ask whether your selected criterion is clearer. Add their brief reply to row 6, or write “not yet checked” if you need another meeting.

**Before you finish:** Explain what you did with the feedback and why, or what still needs clarification. Keeping a feature with reasons can be just as thoughtful as changing it.

**Ways to take part:** Write, type, sketch, speak, sign, or use a communication board or device (AAC), whichever works for you. Take time to prepare, and keep the reading, math and communication supports you need. If someone writes for you, check that they wrote what you meant. For work kept somewhere else, such as a recording or a drawing, add a short note in your portfolio saying where it is. Need words to start? Open **Sentence Starters for Explaining and Responding**.

**Find your way:** Open **My Resources**, then **Unit Map: Four Lessons, One Portfolio**, to reach your portfolio or another lesson. Do not delete earlier entries.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Communicating High Expectations to Learners”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/communicating-high-expectations-to-learners) (Novak Education, 2024). This is an original AlloFlow lesson; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

history.data:
## What does your own work show?

**Today:** Explain your thinking now, then decide what to carry forward. Complete portfolio rows **7 · Final response** and **8 · Evidence + next check**.

### 1. Explain your thinking now

Keep **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** open. Use the same needed supports and criteria: **Reasoning** (how facts support your choice) and **Case checks** (cost, shelf routes and untested effects). You may compare the two starting plans again or choose your own pair. You may consult your earlier notes. Explain your current reasoning in your own words in **7 · Final response**: compare two plans, show the cost, explain two case facts with reasons, and name a remaining check. Your purchase choice does not have to change.

### 2. Look back and choose a next step

Now open your first response and your exchange or feedback records. In **8 · Evidence + next check**, use three short parts. Notes, a labeled sketch, a short letter to your teacher, an audio or video recording, or a poster can all work.

- **My work shows…** Point to one example in the first and final response for **Reasoning**, then for **Case checks**. What is clearer, still strong or still uncertain? No change is an honest finding.
- **Working with someone…** Look back at your personal discussion goal from row 2. Choose one actual reply or piece of feedback. Explain what it helped you notice, what remained unclear, or why it was not useful. Name one strength or strategy you used and a challenge that remains. If the exchange is missing, say so and arrange a chance to try it.
- **Next time I will…** Name another time you could use a strategy that helped, a support you will keep, and how you will tell whether it helped.

### 3. Share one useful discovery

Choose one part to share with a partner or educator. With your partner, also name one thing that helped you decide together and one thing you would change about how you worked. Ask one question if you want help understanding what your work shows. You do not need to share private details. You may also suggest a clearer reflection prompt or a response method that would help you next time.

**Before you finish:** Keep your first and final work, and identify one next action you can try.

**Ways to take part:** Write, type, sketch, speak, sign, or use a communication board or device (AAC), whichever works for you. Take time to prepare, and keep the reading, math and communication supports you need. If someone writes for you, check that they wrote what you meant. For work kept somewhere else, such as a recording or a drawing, add a short note in your portfolio saying where it is. Need words to start? Open **Sentence Starters for Explaining and Responding**.

**Find your way:** Open **My Resources**, then **Unit Map: Four Lessons, One Portfolio**, to reach your portfolio or another lesson. Do not delete earlier entries.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“It’s Always Time for Student Self-Reflection”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/student-self-reflection) (Novak Education, 2025). This is an original AlloFlow lesson; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

Give your recommendation, cost, two case facts with reasons, and one remaining check. Use your needed supports. Keep this first try. Complete two named rows per session; Summary and Connections are optional.
Lesson 1. Keep one agreed example of a criterion. Explain how you and your partner will send, receive and check ideas; try the method. Add one personal discussion goal for the unit.
Lesson 2. Keep one actual chain: my idea → partner reply → my response. Check together that it says what each person meant. If needed, mark “still waiting” and arrange another chance.
Lesson 2. Keep a copy or reference to the shared recommendation: cost, two facts with reasons, what your partner’s idea changed, and one remaining check. If you still disagree, write down both ideas.

Lesson 3. Choose Reasoning (how facts support the choice) or Case checks (cost, shelf routes and untested effects). Point to one place in your work. Write what the reviewer said and what you think it means; ask them to confirm or correct it.
Lesson 3. Keep the part you changed, or explain why you kept it, with a case fact and a remaining check. Add the reviewer’s reply, or “not yet checked”. Keep your earlier version.

Lesson 4. You may consult earlier notes. In your own words, explain your current comparison and recommendation: cost, two case facts with reasons, and one remaining check. Use the same criteria and needed supports.

Lesson 4. Three short parts:
My work shows… Compare a first/final example for Reasoning, then Case checks. What is clearer, the same, or still unsure?
Working with someone… Look back at your personal goal from row 2. Use an actual reply or feedback example. What helped, remained unclear or was not useful? Name a strength or strategy you used and a remaining challenge.

data.essentialQuestion: How can we explain a decision, learn from another idea, and use our work to choose a next step?
objectives: Explain a comparison and recommendation using two relevant case facts and reasons.
Check the fictional constraints and identify a remaining question.
Respond to an actual contribution, use feedback, and reflect with examples from work.
materialsNeeded: The Unit Map, the Case Sheet (Evidence A–E, prices and criteria), four lesson pages, and one personal Decision Portfolio per learner.
A partner or educator for real exchanges, familiar reading and communication tools, and time to prepare and respond.
Optional cut-paper visual models for Lesson 3, the optional Sentence Starters chart, and Words for This Unit. No furniture purchase, room redesign, or physical materials are required.
data.hook:
## Why this unit

Katie Novak’s articles on high expectations, academic discourse and self-reflection share practical advice: make the goal clear, build success criteria with learners, give feedback they can act on, and leave time to revise and reflect. This unit applies that advice across four short sessions around one shared decision.

## Choose the route that fits your group

Use this four-session unit when you want sustained practice with goals, feedback and reflection. It revisits one fictional case across four sessions of roughly 35–45 minutes. The shorter **Thinking Together: A Reading-Space Decision** lesson introduces the same discussion goal in two shorter sessions. Choose either route; completing both is optional. Students who already know the case can record their current thinking as their first response.

**More practice later:** After either route, the separate **Thinking Together: More Practice** pack (alloflow.dev/p/reading-space-practice) offers six optional follow-up routes, including one where learners bring a real class decision.

## Before students begin

**Review first.** Before teaching, review the source alignment, challenge, examples, case arithmetic, pacing, access, and the student view. Check that pictures and descriptions support the captions without adding facts beyond the written case. Confirm that learners can navigate, keep earlier work, and respond through workable methods. Adapt the timing after this review.

1. **Check readiness.** Learners need a way to compare two short plans, add prices up to six tokens, and identify a case fact. Model unfamiliar task words and provide reading or arithmetic support as needed. The learning goal is reasoning and responding; fluent reading, handwriting, or mental calculation are not entry requirements.
2. **Choose a workable recording setup.** Each learner keeps one portfolio. On shared devices, agree where each person’s individual first/final responses will live before starting. The notebook fields store text; speech, signing, AAC, audio or sketches can be kept in the learner’s usual approved format with a short reference in the portfolio. A recorder checks with each learner that the notes say what they meant. Agree how learners will show or share their portfolio for feedback; saving on the device does not submit work to the teacher.
3. **Open the prepared resources.** Everything in this unit works without an AI account. In student view, open **My Resources**; in teacher view, use **Class & Materials**. Demonstrate opening the Unit Map and returning to the portfolio, then verify that each learner can keep earlier work.
4. **Preserve the first attempt.** Offer access and task-wording support for both individual responses. Save the first response before showing the fictional model or supplying content feedback. In Lesson 4, learners may consult their earlier notes while explaining their current reasoning in their own words. This is a formative comparison, not a memory test or a controlled pretest.

**Reduce decision overload.** The Case Sheet offers two unworked starting plans: lamp + basket (3 tokens) and divider + basket (4). Learners may use these or create a pair. The reasons remain theirs to develop; no single purchase is the answer. Arithmetic and reading supports do not lower the reasoning goal.

**Using a resource separately:** Provide the Case Sheet with any lesson or the portfolio. The illustrated comparison restates its essential facts; the full case remains necessary for learners’ own decisions. Evidence letters are reference labels, not definitions.

**Keep recording manageable.** Each session uses two portfolio rows. Brief notes or references to approved recordings are sufficient; no transcript or polished essay is required. In row 4, each learner keeps a copy or reference to the shared recommendation. In row 6, save only the changed part, or the reason for keeping it, not a complete recopy. Summary and Connections remain optional.

**Using it with other grades:** The case suits grades 5–8. For grade 5, read the Case Sheet together and start from the two starter plans. For grades 7–8, ask for a comparison of three plans or a short written justification. You can also swap in a real decision your class faces, such as a library layout or a class event, and keep the same moves. Keep the same goal at every grade: a reason linked to evidence, and a real response to another person’s idea.

**Fading the starters:** In Lessons 1–2, offer whole sentence starters. In Lesson 3, invite learners to try just the first words. In Lesson 4, invite their own wording, with the starters still on hand. Fade the starters, never the access supports (AAC, reading tools, thinking time).
data.directInstruction:
## Criteria learners can use

Use the full labels **Reasoning**, **Case checks**, and **Responding**. Invite learners to propose one concrete example of a criterion and check its meaning together. Keep the same thinking goal and the access supports learners need across the first and final responses.

### Keeping the case facts and access supports clear

All case quantities and findings are invented. In the preferences record, choices overlap; do not total them as separate people. A divider has no established sound effect. A lamp serves one position. The teacher checks actual routes, fit and placement before any real use. Do not assess eye contact, pace, voice volume, handwriting, tool choice or fewer supports. Invite task-focused reflections without asking learners to disclose private needs or diagnoses.

Before the first individual response, explain the words *recommendation* (a choice with reasons), *evidence* (information used to support or question an idea; here, use the fictional case facts), and *criterion* (what we look for in useful work), if needed. Invite learners to restate these meanings. Keep case-answer feedback for after that first response; never withhold reading, communication or task-wording support.
data.guidedPractice:
## Facilitate the four sessions

These are flexible 35-minute starting allocations, not deadlines. Allow up to 45 minutes or split a session for reading, thinking, communication or feedback. Keep the same goal.

- **Lesson 1 — rows 1–2:** 10 minutes for the warm-up, reading the Case Sheet and clarifying task words; 12 for the first response; 10 to develop a criterion example and test the exchange method; 3 to check records. Save the first attempt before content feedback. If it is incomplete, keep it as a starting point and teach the next step.
- **Lesson 2 — rows 3–4:** 7 minutes to model and notice a useful reply; 12 for the actual exchange; 13 to make and record the working decision; 3 to explain what a reply clarified or left unresolved. Model a question, receive its answer and respond to that meaning before sending pairs off.
- **Lesson 3 — rows 5–6:** 7 minutes to compare the two visual examples; 10 for one focused feedback conversation; 12 to try the next version; 6 to return to the reviewer. A learner may retain a feature with reasons. Arrange a later check when the return conversation is unfinished.
- **Lesson 4 — rows 7–8:** 12 minutes for the final response; 15 for the three-part reflection; 8 to share a selected discovery and choose a next action. Point learners to the work already saved rather than asking for an additional report.

**When time is tight:** End at the current named row and resume there. Protect the actual exchange and time to act on feedback; the written volume is flexible. The short visual comparison and closing share can be teacher-facilitated. Do not require every learner to speak publicly.

**Go deeper choices:** Offer the extension choices below to every learner who wants them, not only to those who finish first. Use the same criteria for any of them.

### What counts as useful evidence?

For Reasoning, inspect a comparison and the links between two case facts and reasons. For Case checks, inspect the total, no repeated items, route check and a limit the evidence supports. For Responding, examine an actual meaning-related reply and its effect. Use descriptions such as evidenced here, needs another check, or not observed; these are our formative notes, not source-defined levels. Do not infer individual mastery from a group recommendation.

**Choose a next prompt after the first response is saved.** For the final response, learners may consult their notes but explain the reasoning themselves.

**Facts listed without a reason:** Ask, “Why does that fact favor this plan over the other?” Invite the learner to add one fact-to-comparison link in their own words.

**An untested sound effect stated as certain:** Ask, “What does the sound-check record or equipment description tell us, and what still needs checking?” Invite the learner to state the limit and name a check.

**Two contributions with no meaning-related reply:** Ask, “What actual reply addressed the first message’s meaning?” Arrange an opportunity to check and respond to that meaning. Record “not yet observed” if the exchange has not occurred; do not supply or invent it.

Choose one next step, receive the learner’s response, and check it against the same criterion. A different purchase, more edits or a fluent response is not automatically stronger evidence.

### Sample strong first response (teacher reference only)

Use this to calibrate your feedback. Do not show it before learners save their own first response.

“I compared lamp + basket (3 tokens) with divider + basket (4 tokens). I recommend lamp + basket. Evidence D says the corner light does not reach every reading position, and a lamp adds light at one position, so it helps with a problem we know about, at one reading spot. It will not light every seat. Evidence C says nobody has tested whether a divider reduces sound, so I would rather try separate times for quiet reading and partner discussion than spend 3 tokens on a divider that might not help. Total: 3 tokens, each item once. Still to check: whether the basket and the lamp cord keep the route to every shelf clear.”

**Why it is strong:** it compares two plans, links two facts to reasons, shows a correct total, does not claim the divider blocks sound, and names a route check. A response that recommends the divider can be just as strong if its reasons are this clear.
data.independentPractice:
## Accept honest results

### Must there be a changed decision or a successful retry?

No. Accept justified retention and accurate reports of uncertainty. Ask what the evidence supports. A missing reply needs another opportunity, not an invented exchange. Review the first/final individual work for Reasoning and Case checks; use the actual exchange records separately for Responding. The comparison is formative.

**Interpret reflection proportionately.** A first/final comparison is a conversation about this work, not a controlled measurement of growth. The teacher checks whether work and exchange evidence support the claim, and asks one clarifying question where needed. No change, unresolved disagreement or a missing reply can be reported honestly. Invite learners to suggest a clearer reflection prompt or response option without changing the reasoning goal.

## Sources and attribution

### How does this unit relate to Katie’s writing?

This is an original AlloFlow companion draft informed by three public blog posts: [Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration); [Communicating High Expectations to Learners](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/communicating-high-expectations-to-learners); [It’s Always Time for Student Self-Reflection](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/student-self-reflection). Katie did not author or endorse this unit. The case, model, criteria, timing and portfolio are our teaching choices. The original discourse pack remains a separate optional resource.

### Which source materials are not included?

No companion discourse guide, downloaded flowchart, site image, prompt table, or third-party rubric is reproduced. The self-reflection article credits teacher feedback and an adapted Best-Future.org rubric. Our portfolio and criteria are independent original designs. Follow the article links for the source texts and their credits.

### Which ideas each lesson uses

Each student lesson ends with a short credit line. This is what each lesson takes from Katie’s articles:

- **Lesson 1** (“Communicating High Expectations to Learners”): a clear goal with success criteria built together with learners (her strategies 1 and 2), including the “I can” checks on the Case Sheet, and grade-level challenge with scaffolds (strategy 8).
- **Lesson 2** (“Beyond Turn & Talk”): modeling a useful reply, thinking time, talk moves, multiple ways to communicate, and a shared decision that can need both partners’ evidence.
- **Lesson 3** (“Communicating High Expectations to Learners”): action-oriented feedback and time to revise (strategy 4).
- **Lesson 4** (“It’s Always Time for Student Self-Reflection”): reflecting with examples from work, a choice of response formats, and inviting learners to suggest better prompts.

## UDL design and standards

### How this unit applies UDL

The unit follows a core Universal Design for Learning idea: keep the goal firm and make the ways of reaching it flexible. The goal stays the same in all four sessions: explain a decision with case evidence, respond to another idea, use feedback, and compare first and final work. The notes below use the three principles of CAST’s UDL Guidelines (version 3.0).

- **Engagement (the why of learning).** The first try is ungraded and kept; learners may use a starter pair of plans or build their own; keeping a plan with reasons counts as much as revising it; learners can suggest a clearer reflection prompt.
- **Representation (the what of learning).** The full case sits on one Case Sheet used in every lesson; criteria use full names (Reasoning, Case checks, Responding) with a co-built example; key task words are defined before the first response; every picture is optional and fully captioned.
- **Action and Expression (the how of learning).** Speech, writing, typing, signing, AAC and sketches all count, with a short portfolio note pointing to work kept elsewhere; arithmetic and reading supports do not lower the reasoning goal; optional sentence starters support each lesson.
- **Learner agency.** The portfolio lets learners compare their own first and final work and choose a next check, the self-monitoring UDL aims to build.

**When you adapt:** change the means freely: timing, grouping, recording format and supports. Keep the goal. If a support starts doing the reasoning for the learner, such as a completed starter they copy, it has changed the goal.

### Standards

The unit addresses these grade 6 Common Core standards:

- **SL.6.1:** take part in collaborative discussions, building on others’ ideas and expressing your own clearly. *Lessons 1–4, centred on the Lesson 2 exchange.*
- **SL.6.1.A:** come prepared and refer to evidence. *Lessons 1–2, using the Case Sheet.*
- **SL.6.1.B:** follow agreed discussion rules, set goals and define roles. *Lesson 1: agreeing how to exchange ideas and setting a personal discussion goal; Lesson 2: taking turns to start and respond.*
- **SL.6.1.C:** ask and answer specific questions that add to the discussion. *Lessons 2–3: replying to a partner and asking for feedback.*
- **SL.6.1.D:** review key ideas and show understanding of other perspectives by reflecting and paraphrasing. *Lesson 2 meaning checks and Lesson 4 reflection.*
- **W.6.1.B:** support a claim with clear reasons and relevant evidence. *The first and final recommendations (portfolio rows 1 and 7).*

Any communication method counts: writing, typing, signing, AAC or a scribe. For W.6.1.B, a dictated or scribed recommendation shows the same reasoning as a handwritten one.

successCriteria: Reasoning: I can compare two plans and explain how two case facts support my choice.

Case checks: I can show a total of 6 tokens or fewer with each item chosen once, say how I would check the shelf routes, and name one question that is still open. I don’t claim something works when no one has tested it.
Responding: I can check that I understood what my partner actually said, answer it, and show what my reply changes or leaves open.
